Autopilot: set the course and the ship steers to it with up to 20° of rudder. Hand steering: choose the rudder angle in the Hand steering box; the ship keeps turning until you put the rudder back to 0. The telegraph keys set the engine order; the ship takes time to gain and lose speed, and runs on a long way with the engine stopped.

Press HAND STEERING in the Own ship box first. Then press an angle: minus is port, plus is starboard. The − and + keys at the ends change the order by 1°. The rudder takes time to move to the order.

DEFAULT SETTINGS puts the controls in the known starting state every radar offers: X band, 6 NM, rings off, one EBL and one VRM (0.25 NM) on, true motion north-up, ground stabilised, trails 6 min, relative vectors of 6 min, automatic acquisition off, AIS on, CPA limit 2 NM and TCPA limit 12 min. Gain, clutter and tuning are left as they are.

Display
Steering gear
Ship

Day: dark-blue picture, yellow echoes, white graphics. Night: black picture with everything dimmed, so the display does not spoil night vision on the bridge. Telemotor 1 is the primary steering gear unit and always runs: the rudder then takes 28 seconds from hard over to hard over. With telemotor 2 running as well it takes 18 seconds. Every new scenario starts on telemotor 1 only.

Control panel

FunctionKey

A hardware panel that acts as a keyboard works the radar with these keys: press "Set", then the key (or turn the knob one click) that should do it. Esc leaves it unchanged. A box of knobs that acts as a game controller needs no setting up: its first four knobs are gain, sea clutter, rain clutter and brilliance. The keys do nothing while you are typing in a box. The starting keys are this simulator's own choice, not those of any maker's radar.

The fixed data and the draught, cargo, destination and ETA are typed in, as on a ship's AIS, and are kept on this computer. Position, COG, SOG, heading, ROT and UTC come from the simulation. In the real areas the depth is the approximate depth of water below mean sea level where the ship is (a world relief model with cells of about 450 m, no tide; not reliable near the coast), and under the keel when the draught is known: a guide only, and the ship never touches bottom. The position is counted from a made-up starting point (the scenarios are not tied to a real chart). The starting values are placeholders, not a real ship.

Communications (VHF, typed)

Sound signals

Whistle signals of the collision regulations. Rule 34, vessels in sight of one another: 1 short blast, altering to starboard; 2 short, to port; 3 short, astern propulsion; 5 short, in doubt. Rule 35, restricted visibility: 1 prolonged blast when making way, 2 prolonged when under way but stopped, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes. A short blast is about 1 second, a prolonged blast 4 to 6 seconds. The pitch follows the ship's length. Each signal is written in the exercise record.

Parallel index lines (true bearing of the line; distance off, + to starboard of that bearing)

Ahead and astern cut a line short: how far it runs from the point abeam of own ship, along the line and back. Leave them blank for a full line. HDG puts that line parallel to the ship's heading.

Route, search pattern and charted coastline

Route: press "add waypoints", click the waypoints in order, press again when done. The route is fixed to the ground. The EBL / CURSOR panel then shows the next waypoint, its bearing and distance, and XTD, the distance off the leg being sailed (S to starboard of it, P to port). A search pattern is a route made for you from a datum: an expanding square (legs of 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 ... times the track spacing, every turn 90° to starboard) or a sector search (three triangles through the datum, every turn 120° to starboard). The charted coastline is the coast as the simulator has it, drawn as a line: land that is low or hidden paints less on the radar than the chart shows. The outline sheet is the same coastline with a latitude and longitude grid, for plotting position lines by hand: it is not a chart. The depth contours (5, 10, 20, 30, 50 and 100 m; to 10 m solid, deeper dashed) are drawn from a world relief model with cells of about 450 m, below mean sea level and with no tide: banks, reefs and dredged channels smaller than that are not in it and near the coast it is not reliable. They are a guide for comparing the radar with the lie of the bottom, not a chart.

Offset EBL: press "EBL origin", then click the point it should start from (it stays at that position). Press again to return it to own ship. Nav lines: press "draw", click the points of a line (a channel edge, a limit), press again to end the line; draw as many lines as needed. They are fixed to the ground, so use them on a ground-stabilised picture. Saved maps are kept on this computer. Off-centring works in relative motion. S band sees through rain and sea clutter better, but small craft and buoys are detected at shorter range and SARTs (and X-band racons) do not answer. Detection ranges follow IMO MSC.192(79) table 2; the band and pulse figures shown are typical values, not those of a particular set.

Tick the EBL or VRM: the line appears and follows the cursor over the display (drag on a touch screen). Double-click or double-tap the display to LOCK it where it is. Use "Move EBL" / "Move VRM" to unlock it again, or fine-tune with the slider (moving the slider also locks it). With neither free, a single click on an echo puts both on it and locks them. The bearing shown is true.

Radar controls

50
50
0
0
70

The pulse repetition frequency normally follows the pulse length (short 3000, medium 1500, long 600 a second). Chosen by hand, a lower PRF puts fewer pulses on each target, so weak echoes are lost sooner, and it lengthens the range measured without ambiguity (150,000 km divided by the PRF), so second-trace echoes move or disappear. A PRF too high for the pulse length in use is greyed out: the transmitter could not keep it up. On most sets the PRF is not a control of its own.

A long pulse gives stronger echoes but poorer range discrimination and a larger minimum range; a short pulse the reverse. The performance monitor paints a plume astern: compare its length with the dashed arc, which is the length when the set was new. Echo averaging hides echoes that come and go (a small boat or buoy in a seaway), echo stretch can hide small or fast targets, and interference rejection costs very weak echoes a little: do not leave them on without need.

Tune for the highest meter reading. The best tuning point changes each time you restart.

Environment

3
80

Refraction changes how far the radar sees over the horizon: in sub-refraction (cold air over a warmer sea, bad weather) targets are detected at about 80% of the usual range; in super-refraction (warm dry air over a cooler sea, settled weather) at up to about 140%. Ducting carries the beam much further and brings second-trace echoes.

"Keep the collision regulations": a ship that has to give way to own ship alters to starboard in good time; a stand-on ship holds on, and acts herself only at the last moment if own ship does nothing; in restricted visibility each alters to starboard for own ship forward of her beam; when past and clear she goes back to her course. "One gets it wrong": the first ship to act turns to port instead, as ships sometimes do. Exercises are written and marked for ships that keep their course and speed, so leave it at that unless the instructor wants otherwise. The ships' manoeuvres are written in the record for the instructor; the trainees are not told.

100

Tidal stream table (tidal diamonds)

The sea comes from the direction of the wind (from the west if no wind is set). A ship with a manoeuvring model rolls, pitches and yaws in it: most roll in a beam sea, most yaw with the sea on the bow or quarter. Heavy rolling tips the radar beam and weakens echoes abeam; yawing smears a head-up picture. The exercise ship is not moved by the sea.

The tidal stream is added to the steady current. It is zero at slack water, strongest about 3.1 hours later, slack again at 6.2 hours and then runs the other way (ebb).

Waves slow a ship with a manoeuvring model and the larger target ships, most in a head sea, once the loss is more than her sea margin (about 5% of her speed); a beam sea pushes her sideways a little. A swell rolls and slows her as a wind sea does, but makes no sea clutter. Tide on: the tidal streams of the tidal diamonds (by the hour from high water, between springs and neaps, and between the diamonds) are added to the current, and the echo sounder reads the charted depth plus the height of the tide (rule of twelfths). The real areas' tables are INVENTED for training, not from any chart or tide table.

ARPA operation

100

    Standby clears every target and switches the ARPA off. The self-test checks the ARPA's own calculations against test targets with known answers and checks the gyro and log inputs. A bottom-track log measures speed over the ground, so "sea" stabilised true vectors then show motion over the ground. Sound starts after the first click on the page.

    AIS targets

    The AIS display is off for this manual plotting exercise: plot the targets from the radar alone. It can be switched on again after Finish.

    Sleeping AIS targets closer than the range chosen are activated by themselves. With automatic acquisition on, an AIS target in an acquisition zone is activated too, with a NEW AIS TARGET warning. A dangerous target is always activated. At most 40 targets can be activated: a caution comes at 38, and a further activation is refused with a warning.

    Filter for sleeping targets

    Filter off: every sleeping target is drawn.

    The filter thins out a crowded picture: a sleeping AIS target is not drawn when any criterion that is set says it is of no interest (further off, passing wide or opening, its CPA far ahead, or slow). A class on its own does not filter: it narrows the other criteria. Activated, dangerous and lost targets and the selected target are always drawn, and no single target can be taken off the picture; the list below still shows every target. While a filter is on, "AIS FILTER" and the criteria are written at the top right of the picture, and the AIS key reads AIS FILT.

    NameBRGRNGCPATCPACOGSOGState

    Sleeping targets are small triangles. Click a row to activate a target (vector and heading line) and see its data; click again to put it to sleep. A dangerous target is activated automatically. "= R3" means the AIS target and radar track 3 are judged to be the same ship. AIS data is what the other ship transmits: it can be late, wrong or missing, and small craft and buoys have none.

    Vectors

    With this on, a target that does not violate the CPA and TCPA limits is tracked but shows no vector. Its vector comes back, with the alarm, when it violates the limits. Switch it off before planning a manoeuvre.

    Sea: true vectors show courses and speeds through the water, from gyro and log. Ground: select a small, isolated FIXED target (buoy, rock, light) in the list or on the screen, then choose Ground. The ARPA then removes that target's apparent motion (the set and drift) to show motion over the ground. If the reference is lost or fades, a POOR GROUND REFERENCE alarm sounds and sea stabilisation returns unless it is restored.

    A dashed vector is PRELIMINARY: the track has not settled, so its CPA and TCPA are not yet reliable.

    Alarms

    Anchor watchNM

    Anchor watch: at anchor, select a tracked target that you know is stationary (a small isolated mark) and press "On, selected target". A warning is given when it has moved more than the distance set from where it was: own ship, or the target, is dragging.

    An ALARM (a dangerous target) sounds until it is acknowledged, flashes until then, and stays shown until the danger has gone. A WARNING gives one short signal, flashes until acknowledged, and is announced again every 5 minutes if it is left. Alerts are acknowledged one at a time: "Acknowledge next" (and the ALARM ACK key) takes alarms first, then the oldest warning. "Silence" stops the sound for 30 seconds without acknowledging anything.
